title: Aaron Feuerstein Keeps Paying His Workers
text:
On the night of December 11, 1995, a fire destroyed most of the Malden Mills textile plant in Lawrence and Methuen, Massachusetts. The family company made Polartec fleece and employed around three thousand people in a region that had already lost much of its industry. Its owner, Aaron Feuerstein, was seventy years old, and the insurance money would have let him close or move production somewhere cheaper.

Instead, a few days later, he announced that he would rebuild in Lawrence and that every worker would keep receiving full pay for the next thirty days. When the month ran out he extended it, and then extended it again. Workers received their wages and health benefits for months while the plant was rebuilt, at a cost to the company of millions of dollars.

The decision made Feuerstein a national figure. He was invited to the State of the Union address and praised by politicians and business writers. Most of the workers came back when the new plant opened.

The story did not end simply. The rebuilding left Malden Mills heavily in debt, and in 2001 the company filed for bankruptcy. Feuerstein lost control of it.
lesson: Loyalty to the people who depend on you can be right even when it is costly, but it is wise to count the cost honestly before you choose.
source: Contemporary press reports (Boston Globe, New York Times, CBS 60 Minutes)
caveat: Analysts disagree about how far the costly rebuilding and payroll decisions contributed to the company's later bankruptcy.
